items.title: Clark Terry interviewed by Joe Williams and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, May 19, 1995
items.q: I’ve had the pleasure of being a friend of yours and very close associate of yours for a very long period of time

ctx.x: Yeah, that one lasted. It still, “Every Day I have the Blues” I do it now. All right. Clark Terry. The man that Ellington said — and Ellington was never wrong, believe me — he said he was “beyond category.” And I am most grateful to be able to call him friend.

Well I’ll tell you Joe, I’ve had the pleasure of being a friend of yours and very close associate of yours for a very long period of time, and I’m looking forward to continuing. So God bless you and straight ahead, and all the best to you.

items.title: Joe Williams interviewed by Leslie Gourse, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996
items.q: when I went with Clark Terry for the State Department. We started the African tour in Sierra Leone.

ctx.x: The Voice of America. And I realized what that really meant when I went with Clark Terry for the State Department. We started the African tour in Sierra Leone. And we were rehearsing prior to the concert that afternoon, and a guy came in in a gray suit, a black guy, and he was saying [sings] “Nobody me — Joe Williams! Joe Williams!” And I thought, I said yeah, there it is, Voice of America, man, Armed Forces Radio. That you were known in second, third world countries all over the world, because of radio and…

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Joe was with the small group.

ctx.x: Did – was Joe Williams working with the band – with the small group too at the Brass Rail? Was he doing things in Chicago?

Yeah. Joe was with the small group. I’ll never forget, because that was the time he bet me and Basie that Ezra Charles was going to beat Joe Louis, and Basie and I laughed at him. He cleaned up on both of us, because Charles did beat him.
Ezra Charles was a big jazz fan. Did you know Ezra Charles?
